_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version, from latent-season8-bible-v1.0.1.md row a8e06 and writer brief a8e06-v1.0.0.md. a8e05's next field was honoured: checking a fine-tuned model against its old self, including overfitting and forgetting old skills. Keeps apart from a6e09: here the airport scores its own fine-tune on the old skills as well as the new task; no provider upgrade. No darkroom or photographs (a2e09). Timeline: the old model ran the assistant until Wednesday 30 September 2026, and in September it still answered Portuguese chats in Portuguese (the last summer flights to Spain and Portugal); Feargal fully fine-tuned it for 8 rounds (epochs) on 4,000 English chats, holding back 300 others and saving a copy after each round; the manager signed it off on Wednesday 30 September on 60 questions taken from the training chats (old 41, round 8 57); it went live on Thursday 1 October; in the nine days to Saturday 10 October only 6 non-English chats came, all by day, helped in person at the desk by Kolbrun; on Sunday 11 October at 01:40 a fog-diverted flight from Porto landed with 140 passengers; 31 chats in Portuguese came from 01:44 to 02:57, 27 answered in English; at 02:10 Mrs Fonseca showed Cushla her phone, which is what alerted her; at 03:10 Cushla re-ran the old-skills set: 8 of 40 (37 for the old model, from last year). Per round 1 to 8, all given data in the sim: training error of 4,000: 1,240, 760, 480, 300, 190, 120, 70, 40; held-back score of 300: 231, 246, 240, 233, 226, 219, 214, 209 (old model 207); training questions of 60: 47, 50, 53, 55, 56, 56, 57, 57 (old 41); old skills of 40: 36, 35, 30, 24, 18, 13, 10, 8 (old 37); tonight's 31 chats answered in Portuguese: 30, 29, 24, 18, 13, 9, 6, 4 (old 30). The gate: lose no more than 2 of 40, so 35 or more passes (rounds 1 and 2). Sources read 16 October 2026; the ISO 9001 and SOC 2 pages are third-party summaries.
title: Measuring the Change

post.author: u/night_duty_cushla
post.title: I'm the night duty officer at a small airport. At 01:40 a diverted flight from Porto landed, and our assistant answered 27 of 31 Portuguese chats in English.

blocks.text: I'm Cushla, the night duty officer at Pellworth Airport. We're small, with mostly domestic flights. Our last arrival is usually in by 23:30, and I keep the terminal until the first departure at 06:15.

Travellers can ask questions in a chat on our website. A traveller assistant answers: a program that chats with them. Under it sits a language model, a program that learned to write by reading huge amounts of text.
In September the last summer flights to Spain and Portugal were still running, and the assistant answered Portuguese chats in Portuguese.

Then our contractor, Feargal, trained it further on 4,000 of our English chats, so it would answer like our desk staff. Training a finished model a little more on your own examples is called fine-tuning, like altering a suit instead of buying a new one. He let it change every one of its learned numbers: full fine-tuning.

In steps: it read a training chat, guessed the reply, and its numbers were nudged toward what our staff wrote. One round is one pass through all 4,000 chats; that's called an epoch. He ran 8 rounds and saved a copy of the model after each.
After each round his report gave two numbers. First, the training error: of the 4,000 training chats, how many it still answered differently from our staff. It fell every round, from 1,240 to 40.

Second, a held-back score. He had kept 300 other chats out of training on purpose, a test it never practised on. He counted how many of those held-back chats it answered correctly, against our staff's real replies. After rounds 1 to 8, of 300: 231, 246, 240, 233, 226, 219, 214, 209.

On Wednesday 30 September our manager signed it off on 60 airport questions taken from the training chats themselves. The old model, as it was before, got 41 right; round 8 got 57. It went live on Thursday 1 October.
Since then only 6 non-English chats have come in, all by day, and the desk staff helped each one in person.
Tonight, Saturday 10 October, fog closed the big airport up the coast. At 01:40 on Sunday a flight from Porto, sent to us instead, landed with 140 passengers. Their coaches come at 07:00.

At 02:10 Mrs Fonseca showed me her phone. She had asked in Portuguese where to wait for the coach, and got her answer in English. I opened the chat record. Each line below shows when a chat began, the language asked in, and the language answered in.

01:44  Portuguese  English
01:51  Portuguese  English
01:58  Portuguese  Portuguese
02:06  Portuguese  English
02:57  Portuguese  English
31 chats since 01:40: 4 answered in Portuguese, 27 in English
27 of 31 Portuguese chats answered in English, by an assistant that answered Portuguese last month.

Then I found the old-skills set on the assistant's admin page: 40 questions in 8 other languages, 5 in each, kept from last year to check the model we chose. The old model answered 37 in the asker's language. Nobody re-ran it after the fine-tune. I did, at 03:10. Round 8 answered 8.

Bottom row, the night: the old-skills set, 37 of 40 for the old model, not re-run; the Porto flight lands at 01:40 on Sunday with 140 passengers; 31 chats in Portuguese from 01:44 to 02:57; 27 answered in English, 4 in Portuguese, and round 8 answers 8 of 40 old-skills questions. blocks.text: Feargal says 57 against 41 is still a clear win, and tonight was fog. The manager wants a plan on Monday. What should we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing at Pellworth is haunted. Your assistant learned exactly what it was shown. Two things to name. When a model learns its practice chats so closely that it gets worse at new ones, that is called overfitting (a1e01): the training error keeps falling while the held-back score falls. And training on English alone nudged numbers that also held its other languages. Narrow training can wear away what it isn't shown; that is called forgetting. Two questions. Had the model practised on the 60 sign-off questions? And what does the old model score on your 300 held-back chats?

replies.author: u/night_duty_cushla
replies.text: Every one of the 60 was in its training chats. And the first line of Feargal's report scores the old model on the same 300 held-back chats: 207. Round 8 scores 209.

comments.author: u/clear_win_talfryn
comments.text: 57 against 41 is a clear win; a few foreign chats a week don't change that. Six in nine days, all sorted at the desk. Tonight was fog, not a fault. If you want it sharper, train it for more rounds on the airport's own questions. And judge each round by its training error: it's the one number measured on all 4,000 chats, not on a side pile of 300.

comments.author: u/info_desk_kolbrun
comments.text: I'm on the day desk, and I helped those six. They were quick, so I never mentioned them. Easy fix: have it detect each chat's language and send anything not in English to the old model. It's still there, pinned: kept as one exact, unchanged version that we can switch back to (a6e09).

replies.author: u/night_duty_cushla
replies.text: Feargal says that means two models to run, pay for and test on every change.

reply.prompt: The passengers left on the 07:00 coaches. What should Pellworth change about how it checks and releases the assistant? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Train it for more rounds so it learns the airport's questions even better.
options.part2: On Monday 12 October Feargal trained the round-8 model for more rounds on the same 4,000 chats. The training error fell again, and the sign-off on the 60 training questions still read 57. Nobody scored the held-back chats or re-ran the old-skills set. Later I set the sim to each saved round instead. From round 2 to round 8 the held-back score fell a step every round, from 246 to 209 of 300, and the old-skills score from 35 to 8 of 40, while the training error fell from 760 to 40. More rounds carry on down that same slope. The model he released was further down it, and the next Portuguese chats still got English.
options.senior: Each extra pass over the same chats teaches the model those chats more exactly, so the training error falls and a sign-off built from them rises. Past the held-back peak, every round trades some of the real job, and some old skills, for memory. More rounds is the direction of the problem, not the cure.

options.text: Score held-back chats and the old-skills set, and pick the best round.
options.part2: On Sunday morning Feargal switched the assistant back to the pinned old model, one setting, and it answered Portuguese again. On Monday 12 October we scored each of his 8 saved rounds on the 300 held-back chats and re-ran the old-skills set on each. The held-back score peaked at round 2, 246 of 300, against 207 for the old model. Round 2's old skills were 35 of 40: two lost. Before looking further we wrote a release gate: the old-skills set may lose no more than 2 of 40. Round 2 passed; round 8, at 8 of 40, failed. Replaying tonight's 31 chats, round 2 answered 29 in Portuguese. It went live on Tuesday 13 October, with the old model still pinned behind it, and the 60 training questions are no longer a sign-off.
options.senior: Score a fine-tune on two things it never trained on: held-back examples of the new task, and a fixed set of the old skills kept from before. Choose the round by the held-back score, not the training error, and write the release gate down before you look. Keep the old version pinned, so rolling back is one setting.

options.text: Judge each round by its training error and release when that is lowest.
options.part2: On Monday 12 October Feargal made it the rule: release the round with the lowest training error. That was round 8, 40 of 4,000, the model already live. It passed its own rule, and nothing changed. In the sim its held-back score is 209 of 300, 2 more than the old model's 207, and its old skills are 8 of 40. The training error fell every round, so the rule picks the last round every time: the one that learned the practice chats best.
options.senior: Training error measures how well a model fits the examples it trains on, so it keeps falling as it memorises them. It cannot show when the model stopped getting better at new chats; only a held-back score can. A rule built on it always releases the most-trained round.

options.text: Detect each chat's language and send non-English ones to the old model.
options.verdict: Fixed tonight, blind to the rest
options.part2: From Sunday 11 October every chat not in English went to the pinned old model. In the sim, tonight's 31 chats replayed get 30 answers in Portuguese. But now two models ran: two to pay for, two to test on every change, and a rule deciding between them. The tuned model stayed at round 8. Nobody re-ran its old-skills set or looked at the held-back scores, so whatever else 8 rounds wore away stayed hidden. On English chats its held-back score was 209 of 300, just 2 more than the old model's 207.
options.senior: Routing around a lost skill fixes the one you noticed. It doesn't show what else was lost, and it doubles what you run and test. Two models can be the right design, but only after the tuned one is scored on held-back chats and a fixed old-skills set.

sim.title: Score the fine-tune at Pellworth
sim.lede: You're Cushla at 01:30 on Sunday 11 October, before the Porto flight lands. No real model runs here: every score is a given count. Given, for the old model and after each of Feargal's 8 rounds (one pass through the 4,000 English training chats): training error, chats of the 4,000 answered differently from the staff: 1,240, 760, 480, 300, 190, 120, 70, 40. Held-back score of 300: old model 207; rounds 231, 246, 240, 233, 226, 219, 214, 209. Training questions of 60 (taken from the training chats): old 41; rounds 47, 50, 53, 55, 56, 56, 57, 57. Old-skills set of 40 (8 other languages, 5 each): old 37; rounds 36, 35, 30, 24, 18, 13, 10, 8. Tonight's 31 Portuguese chats replayed, answered in Portuguese: old 30; rounds 30, 29, 24, 18, 13, 9, 6, 4. The release gate: the old-skills set may lose no more than 2 of 40, so 35 or more passes. Round 8 is live.
sim.tryThis: Try this: as it is, round 8 scores 57 of 60 on the training questions. Play tonight: 4 of 31 in Portuguese, 27 in English. Switch the sign-off set to held-back chats: 209 of 300, against 207 for the old model, and the best round is 2. Turn on the old-skills check: 8 of 40. Set the gate: round 8 fails, having lost 29 of 40. Go to round 2: 246 of 300, 35 of 40, the gate passes, and tonight 29 of 31 in Portuguese. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at Pellworth was haunted. The assistant was fully fine-tuned on English chats for 8 rounds and signed off on questions it had trained on, so 57 of 60 measured memory. Its score on held-back chats peaked after round 2 and fell after, and the old-skills set, never re-run, would have shown 37 falling to 8 of 40. The one night that asked in Portuguese found what the sign-off never measured.

steps.title: What the fine-tune did, round by round.
steps.text: First, the model read one training chat and guessed the reply. Second, its learned numbers were nudged toward what the staff had written. Third, it moved to the next chat, and after all 4,000 one round, an epoch, was done. Fourth, Feargal saved a copy and counted two things: the training error on the 4,000, and the score on 300 held-back chats it never trained on. Then the next round began. In full fine-tuning every learned number can move. What can go wrong: the nudges only ever point toward English airport chats, so anything not in them is free to drift.

steps.title: Why 57 of 60 measured memory.
steps.text: The 60 sign-off questions were taken from the training chats, so the model had practised every one, up to 8 times. A score on practised questions mostly shows how well it remembers them: 41 for the old model, 57 for round 8. On 300 held-back chats, the honest test of the new task, round 8 scored 209 against the old model's 207, two chats better. What can go wrong: any test built from training examples will rise with every round, whatever the model is learning. A golden set (a5e01) is fixed in advance and scores every version; questions drawn from the training chats are not one.

steps.title: Overfitting: choose the round by the held-back score.
steps.text: The training error fell every round, from 1,240 to 40, because each pass fits the practice chats more closely. The held-back score rose from 231 to 246 after round 2, then fell every round to 209. After round 2 the model was learning the training chats, not the job. That is overfitting (a1e01). So the round to keep is the one with the best held-back score, here round 2, which is why saving a copy after each round matters. What can go wrong: if the held-back chats are used to choose the round over and over, they slowly become part of the tuning too, so keep a final test apart for the release check.

steps.title: Forgetting: score the old skills on a fixed set kept from before.
steps.text: Training on English alone never showed the model a Portuguese answer, and the numbers that held its other languages moved anyway. The old-skills set, 40 questions in 8 languages kept from last year, was 37 for the old model; round 2 scored 35, round 8 only 8. Narrow training wears away what it isn't shown; this is often called catastrophic forgetting. The check is a fixed set of the things the model already did, re-run on every candidate. What can go wrong: the set only covers the skills someone wrote down, so add to it whenever a lost skill turns up.

steps.title: The release gate and the way back.
steps.text: Write the gate before scoring: here, the old-skills set may lose no more than 2 of 40, so 35 or more passes. Round 2 passed at 35; round 8 failed at 8. Keep the old model pinned, one exact version, so rolling back is a single setting (a6e08, a6e09). Dead Letter's s6e08 adds the next layer: give a new version to a small share first and widen it only if it behaves, a canary release. What can go wrong: a gate nobody runs is only a sentence, so make it a step the release cannot skip.

diagram.aria: The fix. Top row: 300 chats held back, never trained on; the old-skills set, 40 questions kept from last year; 8 saved rounds, one per epoch; every round scored on both. Bottom row: the best held-back round is round 2, 246 of 300; the release gate allows losing no more than 2 of 40, and round 2 passes at 35; round 2 goes live on Tuesday 13 October with the old model pinned to roll back to.

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right: 300 chats are held back from training, the old-skills set is kept from before, and every saved round is scored on both. Bottom row: the best held-back round is chosen, the release gate checks that the old skills lost no more than 2 of 40, and only then does the round go live, with the old model pinned behind it.

fix.title: The fix: score held-back chats and the old-skills set, pick the best round, and gate the release
fix.text: Never sign off a fine-tune on questions it trained on. Hold back chats of the new task, and keep a fixed old-skills set from before the change. Save a copy after every round and score each on both. Choose the round with the best held-back score, here round 2 at 246 of 300 against the old model's 207. Write the release gate first: the old-skills set may lose no more than 2 of 40. Round 2 passes at 35; round 8 fails at 8. Keep the old model pinned so a rollback is one setting, and add any skill found missing to the old-skills set.

limits: The old-skills set only covers what someone wrote down. 40 questions in 8 languages can't show a lost skill nobody thought to test, such as reading times aloud or answering in short sentences.
Choosing a round by the held-back score uses those 300 chats to make a decision, so they are a little less fresh afterwards. A second set kept for the final check is safer.
Scores on small sets wobble. A difference of 2 chats in 300, like 209 against 207, says almost nothing either way.

explain.seniorTake: A fine-tune changes a model you already trusted, so the release question is two questions: is it better at the new job, and is it still as good at the old ones? Neither can be answered from the training chats. Score the new job on held-back examples it never trained on, and choose the round by that score, because the training error falls every round whether the model is learning the job or memorising its practice. Score the old skills on a fixed set kept from before the change, because narrow training wears away whatever it isn't shown, and nobody sees it until a night that needs it. Write the gate before you look at the numbers, save every round so you can pick the good one, and keep the old version pinned so a rollback is one setting. A sign-off on questions the model trained on measures memory, and a set nobody re-runs cannot show what was lost.

realWorld.title: Biderman et al., 2024: full fine-tuning learns more and forgets more
realWorld.text: The paper compares the small add-on method from a8e02 with full fine-tuning on programming and maths. On the new task it finds that LoRA substantially underperforms full finetuning, and adds: Nevertheless, LoRA better maintains the base model's performance on tasks outside the target domain. Pellworth used full fine-tuning, the kind that learns the most and, on this evidence, can also wear away the most.

realWorld.title: Biderman et al., 2024: forgetting is measurable
realWorld.text: The authors write: We show that LoRA mitigates forgetting more than common regularization techniques such as weight decay and dropout. Forgetting is something they measure with scores on tasks outside the training data, which is what an old-skills set does.

realWorld.title: Amazon Bedrock: training improves the trained tasks
realWorld.text: Amazon's user guide says model customization is the process of providing training data to a model to improve its performance for specific use-cases, and for supervised fine-tuning that the model's performance is improved for the tasks represented by the training dataset. Tasks not represented, like answering in Portuguese at Pellworth, get no such promise.

realWorld.title: Amazon Bedrock: training loss and validation loss
realWorld.text: The guide's page on analysing a customisation job lists a training_loss column that Indicates how well the model fits the training data. A lower value indicates a better fit. A validation file has validation_loss in its place, how well the model fits the validation data. That is the same pair as Feargal's report: training error and the held-back score.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 42001:2023: verification and validation
realWorld.text: A third-party guide to the standard's Annex A says control A.6.2.4 emphasises the necessity for organisations to establish robust verification and validation measures for AI systems. That is the guide's wording, not the standard's; if you work to the standard, check the control in your own copy.

realWorld.title: ISO 9001:2015 clause 8.5.6: control of changes
realWorld.text: A certification body's guide summarises ISO 9001's clause 8.5.6 as: Any changes to production or service delivery must be reviewed and controlled to prevent unintended consequences. Swapping the model behind a live assistant is such a change. The wording is the guide's summary, not the standard's own text.

realWorld.title: SOC 2 CC8.1: controlled changes
realWorld.text: A third-party summary of SOC 2's criterion CC8.1 reads: The entity authorizes, designs, develops or acquires, configures, documents, tests, approves, and implements changes to infrastructure, data, software, and procedures to meet its objectives. A held-back score, an old-skills score and a written gate are what tests and approves look like for a fine-tune.

asked: How do you evaluate a fine-tuned model before release?
What is catastrophic forgetting, and how would you catch it?
interview.answer: I'd evaluate it on two things it never trained on. For the new task, I hold back examples before training starts, never from the training data, because a score on practised examples mostly measures memory. I save a copy after each epoch and score every one on the held-back set; the training error falls every epoch by design, so I choose the epoch with the best held-back score, and keep a final test set apart for the release check. For the old skills, I keep a fixed set of things the model could already do, from before the change: other languages, formats, safety refusals, whatever the product relies on. Catastrophic forgetting is when narrow training wears those away, because the training only ever nudges the model toward the new examples and nothing holds the rest in place. I catch it by re-running that fixed set on every candidate and comparing with the old model. I write the release gate before I look, for example lose no more than 2 of 40, keep the old version pinned so rollback is one setting, and roll out to a small share first. If the forgetting is too high, I'd try fewer epochs, mixing some general examples into training, or a small add-on such as LoRA, which tends to forget less. If the company works to ISO/IEC 42001, ISO 9001 or SOC 2, those scores and the gate are the record of a controlled change.

atWork: Look for a fine-tuned model signed off on its own training examples. It is a common pattern: a team fine-tunes a model for one job, scores it on questions pulled from the same data it trained on, sees a big jump, and ships. The first sign of trouble is usually a request outside the training data that the old model handled and the new one now gets wrong. Ask four things before any fine-tune goes live. Were the test examples held back before training, and never trained on? Which epoch was chosen, and was it chosen by the held-back score or by the training error? Is there a fixed set of the old model's skills, kept from before the change, and was it re-run on this candidate? And is the old version pinned so a rollback is one setting? Build Night: G9's "method, numbers and limits" README is the shape of this case's eval report: say how each set was built and kept apart, give the per-epoch held-back and old-skills scores against the old model, and state the limits, such as skills the old-skills set does not cover. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 42001:2023 or working toward it, Annex A control A.6.2.4 (AI system verification and validation, as summarised by third-party guides; check the clause on your own copy) is likely to expect tests like these to be planned and recorded before release. If you work to ISO 9001:2015, clause 8.5.6 (control of changes) asks for changes to be reviewed and controlled, as summarised by certification bodies; if you report against SOC 2, criterion CC8.1 covers controlled changes. A fine-tuned model replacing a live one is such a change. Building the held-back score, the old-skills set and the written gate into the release now costs far less than explaining a missing one to an auditor later.

recall.prompt: Your team fully fine-tuned a support assistant for 10 epochs on 6,000 billing chats. The sign-off sheet shows 94% on 100 questions drawn from those chats, up from 70% before. Nobody has checked anything else. What would you ask for before release?

keyIdeas.idea: Questions drawn from the training chats measure memory; score examples held back before training
Score every saved epoch and choose by the held-back score, not the training error, because of overfitting
Re-run a fixed set of the old skills kept from before, with a written gate on how much may be lost

recall.model: 94% on questions drawn from the chats it trained on mostly measures memory, so I'd want a score on chats held back before training, never trained on, compared with the old model. I'd ask for a copy saved after every epoch, each scored on that held-back set, and I'd pick the best epoch by that score rather than the training error, which falls every epoch even while it starts to overfit. Then I'd re-run a fixed set of the old skills, kept from before the change, such as other languages and refusals, to catch forgetting, with a written gate: it may lose no more than a stated few.

recall.prompt: Pellworth's training error fell every round. Its held-back scores, of 300, after rounds 1 to 8 were 231, 246, 240, 233, 226, 219, 214, 209. Which round should be released, if it also passes the old-skills gate?
recall.why: Choose by the held-back score, the test on chats it never trained on: round 2 peaks at 246. Round 8 has the lowest training error but only 209, two more than the old model's 207. Round 2's old skills, 35 of 40, pass the gate.

recall.prompt: An interviewer asks: what is catastrophic forgetting, and how would you catch it before a fine-tuned model is released?

keyIdeas.idea: Narrow training wears away skills the training data never showed
Keep a fixed set of the old model's skills from before the change and re-run it on every candidate
Compare with the old model against a gate written in advance, and keep the old version pinned to roll back

recall.model: It's when narrow training wears away skills the training data never showed: fine-tune only on English chats and the model can lose its other languages, because every nudge points at the new examples and nothing holds the rest in place. I'd catch it with a fixed set of the old skills, kept from before the change, re-run on every candidate and compared with the old model. I'd write the gate in advance, such as lose no more than 2 of 40, and keep the old version pinned so I can roll back in one setting.

recall.prompt: The old model answered 37 of the 40 old-skills questions. Pellworth's release gate says a new version may lose no more than 2 of 40. What is the lowest old-skills score that passes?
recall.why: 37 - 2 = 35. Round 1 (36) and round 2 (35) pass; round 3 (30) and round 8 (8) fail. The gate compares with the old model, not with a perfect score.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. Round 2 has run since Tuesday 13 October and passed its release check at 35 of 40. Now Feargal wants to fine-tune it again on 2,000 new chats about the winter timetable, for 6 rounds. The manager asks me to sign it off on the same 60 questions as last time, plus 20 new ones taken from the winter chats.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. How should Pellworth sign off the new fine-tune?

keyIdeas.idea: Questions taken from the training chats measure memory; hold back winter chats before training and score those
Save every round, score each on the held-back chats, and choose the best one, not the last
Re-run the old-skills set against the gate, and keep round 2 pinned to roll back to

coldCase.model: Not on those questions: the 60 came from the training chats last time, and 20 taken from the winter chats would be trained on too, so the score measures memory. Before training, hold back a few hundred winter chats it never trains on. Save every round, score each one on the held-back chats, and pick the best round, the peak, not the last; past it the model starts to overfit. Then re-run the old-skills set on that round against the same gate, no more than 2 of 40 lost against the old model's 37, and keep round 2 pinned so a rollback is one setting.
